extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literature, literary critics, and creative writers interested in archetypal/genre structure
extracted.subtask_description: Analysing and applying Frye's archetypal structural principles for tragedy, comedy, irony, and satire to the practice or critique of literary works; identifies phases, archetypes, and formal functions. Useful for writers shaping genre expectations and critics evaluating genre conformity and effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic Augenblick / crucial moment (cognitio)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy 'moves up to an Augenblick or crucial moment' from which audience can see simultaneously the road to what might have been and the road to what will be; the cognito is normally the recognition of the inevitability of a causal sequence in time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design a clear decisive moment of recognition for the audience (even if the hero is blind to it). Avoid making the 'crucial moment' ambiguous for the audience; ensure causal inevitability is perceptible (foreshadowing, ironies). If the hero is in hubris, the moment should register as dizziness or the start of inevitable decline rather than enlightened insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of time in tragedy vs comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: In tragedy time is bound up with nemesis, cyclical return, and the irreversible passing of potential into actual; in comedy time plays a redeeming role that uncovers what is essential to a happy ending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose how time functions as a structural force: use cyclical or fatalistic temporal images in tragic works (repetition, return, the devouring of life) and progressive, revealing time in comedies (events that expose truth leading to reconciliation). Misusing the wrong temporal logic for the genre undermines its effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy as mimesis of sacrifice (communion and propitiation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy mimics ritual sacrifice: one element is communion (dividing a heroic/divine body to bring unity), the other propitiation (the body belongs to another greater, potentially wrathful power).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embed a paradoxical combination of communal unification and the sense that the hero or body ultimately belongs to a higher power. Use ritual imagery and stages to make the sacrificial dimension felt; avoid treating sacrifice as merely sensational—its communal and propitiatory aspects must be evident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychology of tragedy: Dionysiac vs Apollonian / will to power
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is illuminated by the psychology of the will to power: a 'Dionysiac' aggressive will intoxicated with omnipotence impinging on an 'Apollonian' sense of external, immovable order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Render the conflict between ecstatic/aggressive drives and rigid external order in character psychology and thematic structure. Use this dialectic to motivate hubristic action leading to fall; avoid flattening tragic motive into mere chance or external plot mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catharsis and revelation through the hero's death/fall
rubrics_metrics.description: In tragedy the hero's fall or death often produces a vision of a greater world previously blocked by the hero's spirit and draws survivors into a new unity; at the point of death the hero may become articulate, reviving his song within the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage the hero's demise so it yields communal insight or transformative feeling in survivors/audience. Ensure the death reveals something beyond the hero's previous horizon rather than simply ending action for shock value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy's ritual pattern: death/resurrection and potential for embedded tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy contains a ritual pattern akin to resurrection—the death that precedes epiphany or manifestation of a risen hero; comedy can contain a potential tragedy within itself as part of a total quest-myth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing comedy, consider using symbolic 'deaths' and restitutions (loss and rebirth) to heighten the final reconciliation. If embedding tragic elements, keep them subordinate and structurally oriented toward eventual restoration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural plausibility: difficulty of turning somber action into happy ending
rubrics_metrics.description: It is easy to make a sombre action end happily if not structurally grounded, but the reverse (a comedy turned tragic) is almost impossible without structural basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect genre structural constraints: avoid contrived reversals that violate internal logic. If attempting genre inversion, establish deep structural justification early on so the ending feels earned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic eiron / divine or invisible agent as determinant
rubrics_metrics.description: The withdrawn eiron counterpart in tragedy may be a god (Athene), God the Father, a ghost, or an invisible force whose effects decree the tragic action; it can also be an event prior to the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an authoritative or transcendent agent (personified or impersonal) to crystallize fate or nemesis. Make its presence felt through consequences or prophecy; avoid arbitrary deus-ex-machina interventions late in the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic soothsayer/prophet and Machiavellian villain as catalysts
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic counterpart to the comic tricky slave is the soothsayer/prophet (Teiresias) who foresees the end, and the Machiavellian villain who serves as a catalyzer of tragic action needing minimal motivation (Iago, Bosola).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ prophetic figures to foreshadow inevitability and villains whose internal logic catalyzes catastrophe. Make their motives intelligible as authorial instruments rather than mere caricature; avoid undermotivated agents who break believability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic hero as alazon: hubris and pseudo-divinity
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic hero usually belongs to the alazon group—self-deceived, dizzy with hubris, often beginning as a semi-divine figure whose authority depends on personal ability (tyrannos) rather than pure lawful right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterize tragic protagonists with self-deception and inflated self-regard that sets the stage for dialectical exposure. Show the gradual separation of pretence from actuality; beware of heroes who are simply 'too evil' or purely noble without complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppliant archetype: pathos through exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic suppliant (often female or children) presents unmitigated helplessness and destitution; pathos works by depicting exclusion from the group and invokes the deepest human fears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use suppliant figures to focus pity and terror; ensure their marginalization is meaningful to the social/human stakes of the plot. Avoid using victim figures merely for shock or sentimental manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Messenger / chorus-character functions in tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: A subordinate figure (messenger) often announces catastrophe and focuses the tragic mood; chorus or chorus-characters represent the society from which the hero is isolated and express social norm against which hubris is measured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy messengers and chorus-figures to supply missing cognitio, social perspective, and communal reaction. Keep them distinct from the hero's conscience and avoid letting them serve merely expository functions without social presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy polarizes love and social duty (Antigone archetype)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy typically makes love and social structure irreconcilable—love becomes passion and social activity a forbidding duty (Antigone, Neigung vs Pflicht). Central female figures often polarize the tragic conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set up irreversible conflicts between private bonds and public duty; allow central characters (often women) to embody the moral tension. Avoid flattening the conflict into simple melodrama—its moral ambiguity is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phased structure of tragedy (six phases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy moves through phases: (1) birth/innocence and calumniated woman; (2) youthful innocence/experience lost; (3) paradox of victory/completion; (4) fall by hubris/hamartia; (5) ironic/fatalistic loss of direction; (6) shock/horror and sparagmos (mutilation, torture).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing or evaluating tragedies, map action and tone to the relevant phase(s). Each phase carries distinct expectations (e.g., phase 1 emphasizes innocence vindicated; phase 6 foregrounds horror). Blurring phases is possible but must be justified by structure and theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: First phase of tragedy: birth/innocence and the calumniated woman
rubrics_metrics.description: The first phase gives central dignity to an innocent figure often a calumniated woman whose fidelity is vindicated (examples: Alcestis, Hermione, the Duchess of Malfi).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If adopting phase-one dynamics, center innocence under attack with eventual vindication (or sacrificial restoration). Avoid making the innocence passive—its moral force should be evident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second phase of tragedy: youthful innocence and cut-off lives
rubrics_metrics.description: The second phase is tragedy of youth and inexperience (Romeo and Juliet), often ending with adjustment or education of survivors rather than complete annihilation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict the collision of youthful idealism with adult realities; consider having surviving characters undergo moral growth. Avoid sentimentality—maintain dramatic stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third phase of tragedy: paradox of victory and completion
rubrics_metrics.description: The third phase emphasizes the hero's achievement or completion (the Passion, Samson), producing a paradoxical 'victory within tragedy'—a triumphant end that is tragic in larger context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure narratives where final triumph coexists with larger loss or foreknowledge of doom; ensure the double perspective (local victory vs historical tragedy) is made explicit for audience resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourth phase of tragedy: fall through hubris/hamartia
rubrics_metrics.description: The typical fall of the hero through hubris and hamartia, marking a boundary from innocence to experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chart the moral and psychological errors (hamartia) leading to downfall; make the causal link convincing rather than arbitrary. Avoid portraying the fall as purely accidental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fifth phase of tragedy: ironic/fatalistic loss of direction
rubrics_metrics.description: The fifth phase increases irony, presents characters with lower freedom than the audience, and often involves fatalism or metaphysical questioning (Oedipus Tyrannus, Book of Job).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dramatic irony and settings under law/fate to create a distance between audience knowledge and character ignorance. Avoid over-explaining fatalism—let it emerge through situation and consequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sixth phase of tragedy: shock, sparagmos, and demonic epiphany
rubrics_metrics.description: This phase foregrounds shock and horror, with images of sparagmos (cannibalism, mutilation, torture), demonic visions, prisons, and public spectacles of humiliation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve unqualified horror for works structurally capable of sustaining it; ensure shocking elements serve thematic/dialectical ends rather than mere sensationalism. Beware of false shock (audience resistance masked as outrage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ironic perspective: audience freedom vs character constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Irony is attained by placing characters in a state of lower freedom than the audience; an historical or legal setting (Old Testament, astrology) produces ironic distance for a Christian audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate an authorial or contextual vantage point that grants the audience superior knowledge or freedom, producing irony. Do not confuse irony with mere sarcasm; the structural gap must be sustained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction and overlap of irony and satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire is militant irony: it requires wit/humor founded on fantasy or the grotesque plus an object of attack and at least an implicit moral standard; irony without clear moral standards tends not to be militant satire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define the satiric target and the moral stance underpinning the attack; combine grotesque/fantastic elements with evaluative judgment. Avoid satire that lacks a discernible object or appears as blind invective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain the fantastic/hypothetical tone in satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire (e.g., Swift's Modest Proposal) depends on a fantastic, hypothetically plausible tone—if content becomes oppressively real, satire breaks down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep enough remove or hypothetical framing in satiric argument to preserve ironic distance; do not let brutal realism collapse the comic/fantastic premise and thereby subvert satiric effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire's attack must reach an impersonal level and imply moral standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective attack in satire must reach some impersonal level and thereby commit the attacker, by implication, to a moral standard; mere invective ('flyting') without that is limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame criticism at the level of institutions, vices, or types rather than mere personal abuse. Make the moral criteria explicit or implicit through the selection of absurdities and targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor and convention: cartooning social types
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor is founded on convention; it stylizes the world so that certain character types (obedient wives, professors) are not permitted to exist as realistic full persons within the comic convention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use established comic conventions to set expectations; alter or subvert them consciously. Introducing radically new conventions risks distressing or alienating readers unless carefully signaled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Low-norm satire / counsel-of-prudence tradition
rubrics_metrics.description: The low-norm satire assumes a world full of anomalies yet permanent; it counsels prudence, observation, timing, and conventional behavior (the eiron of the low norm).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For low-norm satire, present common-sense narrators or plain-dealer foils who expose folly via restrained pragmatism. Avoid overreaching moralism—this mode relies on subtle, conventional wisdom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the plain-dealer / eiron as satiric foil
rubrics_metrics.description: The satirist may employ a plain, common-sense conventional person (narrator or rustic) as a foil for society's alazons; this figure corresponds to the plain dealer in comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft a grounded, observational narrator/foil whose understatement or conventionalism illuminates the targets' excesses. Be careful that the foil is credible and not a mere mouthpiece for the author's opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire favors exaggerated alazons as targets
rubrics_metrics.description: In low-norm satire the alazon is a Goliath encountered by a small but astute critic: large, inflated targets (giants) make satiric demolition more effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magnify the target's pretensions to expose their absurdity; hyperbole and caricature can be effective devices. Ensure exaggeration stays tethered to recognizable traits so the satire hits its mark.
